https://www.thewrap.com/industry-news/de.text: Getting your Trinity Audio player ready… Members of the Block the Merger Coalition have sent three separate letters to U.K. Secretary for Culture, Media and Sport Lisa Nandy urging her to formally intervene in the pending $110 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Nandy previously informed Paramount and WBD that she’s “minded” to intervene in the deal while asking for them to address her concerns over whether the deal would result in a “sufficient plurality” of views in news media and address the need for “sufficient plurality of persons with control of the media enterprises, or the enterprises providing on-demand [program] services or both, serving that audience.” The filings from the Democracy Defenders Fund , Archival Producers Alliance (APA) , Documentary Film Council and International Documentary Association (IDA) ask Nandy to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice (PIIN) and refer the merger for a more in-depth Phase 2 investigation with a “view to prohibition or obtaining strong, suitable, structural remedies.” Read Next UK Government ‘Minded to Intervene’ on Paramount-WBD Deal After Review The Block the Merger Coalition warned that the merged entity would become the third-largest linear broadcaster in the U.K. and reach 19% of the population through its on-demand services before accounting for HBO Max. They claimed that the deal would result in the “reduction in the plurality of persons controlling ODPS serving U.K. audiences,” citing CEO David Ellison’s plans to combine Paramount+ and HBO Max into a single platform. They also said that the merger would hand a single owner a significant proportion of children’s linear channels operating in the U.K. that could be consolidated into Paramount and extinguish a significant presence in the market; would put the CNN and CBS News archives under a single owner and “worsen discretionary gatekeeping of archival materials,” impacting U.K. documentarians’ ability to tell diverse stories; and would bring Channel 5 News, CBS News, CNN and CNN International under the common ownership of a single controlling family and could potentially “eliminate at least one distinct voice in the U.K. market for international and U.S. news programming.” APA represents over 700 archive producers from around the globe, while IDA represents over 3,500 documentary professionals across 75 countries. Read Next Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Cleared by European Commission With Conditions The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority will decide on whether it will clear the merger, seek remedies or launch a Phase 2 investigation by Aug. 7. Meanwhile, the deal has been cleared by the U.S. Department of Justice , Warner Bros. shareholders and the European Commission , who implemented conditions such as an exit from United International Pictures. Other countries where the deal has received clearance or where relevant waiting periods have expired include Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, South Africa, Ukraine, Montenegro, New Zealand and North Macedonia. Foreign direct investment authorities in Spain, Germany, Slovenia, Belgium, Czechia, Italy, France and Romania have also signed off. In addition to the U.K., Paramount’s litigation with the 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America will move to an antitrust trial , with the date for a specific hearing to be announced. The media giant agreed to delay the closing of its merger until five days after the outcome of a trial or June 1, 2027, whichever is earliest. A Paramount shareholder and a group of consumers also filed separate lawsuits to block the merger, though the latter was denied a preliminary injunction after a judge ruled that they failed to show irreparable harm or that their case would have a likelihood of success. In the event the transaction does not close by Sept. 30, WBD shareholders will receive a 25 cent per share “ticking fee” for each quarter until closing , which translates to a payout of roughly $650 million per quarter, or $7 million per day. In the event that the deal does not close at all due to regulatory matters, Paramount will pay WBD a $7 billion termination fee. Read Next Paramount Agrees to Push Warner Bros. Merger as Far Back as Summer 2027

Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romanian authorities do not currently expect problems with fuel supplies for households, agriculture, or transport companies, interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan said on Tuesday, August 4. His comments came after three government meetings on the country's energy situation, fuel supplies, and measures to maintain the stability of the national power system. Ilie Bolojan, who is also the acting minister of energy, said the situation had improved, with the OMV refinery processing at full capacity and Petromidia operating at around 85% of capacity. The latter is expected to return to normal operations by the end of the week. “At this moment, we do not anticipate problems regarding fuel supplies for the population, agriculture and transport operators," Bolojan said. The assurances come amid a sharp rise in fuel prices. Diesel has climbed above RON 10.80 per liter in Bucharest after more than a week of sustained increases, while gasoline is selling for more than RON 9.50 per liter at some filling stations, Euronews Romania reported. According to the broadcaster, Romania recorded the highest increase in fuel prices in the European Union over the past week, at 7.5%, adding around RON 57 to the cost of a full tank. In this context, president Nicușor Dan announced on Tuesday that he had signed the decree promulgating legislation introducing measures aimed at stabilizing the petroleum products market amid rising fuel prices. "Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and extreme volatility on the international oil market have generated rapid increases in fuel prices, including in our country," Dan said. "Rapid state intervention was once again necessary because these price increases translate into higher costs throughout the economy for citizens and businesses, with direct effects on purchasing power, economic competitiveness, and the stability of critical national sectors." According to the president, the legislation provides for declaring a crisis situation on the petroleum products market, reducing the excise duty on diesel, capping commercial markups, and temporarily banning diesel exports without prior approval from the Energy Ministry in order to prioritize domestic consumption. It also introduces a solidarity contribution for large oil companies. The government also reviewed the situation at the Cernavodă nuclear power plant amid low Danube levels. Dredging and rock removal works are continuing, while an operation involving the sinking of barges is planned once all technical conditions are met. The measures are intended to extend the operation of Unit 2 for as long as possible, according to the prime minister. “The water level at Cernavodă has not fallen further. This is a good sign, but the situation remains difficult, and we are continuing all measures to keep the unit operating for as long as possible," Bolojan said. "Every day of operation means additional energy for the National Energy System.” The prime minister also met with major electricity suppliers to discuss measures aimed at maintaining balance in the energy system. The talks covered ways of ensuring market liquidity through the payment of outstanding amounts under the compensation scheme, as well as cooperation with grid operator Transelectrica on voluntary reductions in electricity consumption by large industrial consumers. The government also agreed with energy regulator ANRE to accelerate the issuance of documents required for projects already at an advanced stage, allowing new power generation capacity to come online as quickly as possible. At the same time, the government is preparing a backup mechanism that could temporarily limit electricity consumption by major industrial users if voluntary reductions prove insufficient during peak hours. “In the coming days, we will adopt a government decision implementing the mechanism provided by law for situations in which voluntary consumption reductions are not sufficient to cover electricity demand during peak hours," Ilie Bolojan said. Under the mechanism, large consumers could receive 24 hours' notice of temporary consumption limits, depending on the nature of their operations and the capacity of the National Energy System. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Gov.ro) Read next 04 August 2026 Transport Dacia and Ford halt production for maintenance as Romania seeks to cut energy use, PM says Normal Energy Romanian PM says no fuel supply problems expected as energy system remains under pressure 04 August 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? https://www.dw.com/en/us-charges-5-peopl.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MfsF The DOJ unsealed the charges one day after DW published an investigation into one of the members of the network, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy Image: LRT Advertisement The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has charged five men with working for Russian intelligence to carry out surveillance and plan targeted killings in the United States and Europe . "The men were recruited to carry out attacks and assassinations around the world, including the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment. Yuri Khrameev, 63, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, both Russian nationals; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy , 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela , 22, were charged with an alleged conspiracy to commit financial terrorism. Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. All the individuals are still at large. The DOJ announced the unsealing of charges against the five individuals one day after DW published an investigation looking into one of the members of the murder plot. The DW investigation identified Romagoza Durruthy as a salsa teacher in Russia who recruited a number of people in 2024 to carry out sabotage across Europe. The agents were mostly from Spanish-speaking countries and had been sent across Europe to commit arson attacks on businesses and military equipment destined for Ukraine. The investigation found that Romagoza Durruthy had been the person who directed them and organized their travels. How a Cuban dance teacher aided Russian sabotage in EU To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What else did the DOJ say? Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the plans included attempts to assassinate a Russian dissident in Washington, DC. According to the DOJ, several people were recruited in the US alone to surveil Russian dissidents, in addition to monitoring civilian and military infrastructure in European countries such as Lithuania . The Justice Department also reported that one recruit was allegedly offered "$40,000 to 'eliminate' or 'disappear' a US resident." Last year, another recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania. Russia has previously denied carrying out such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States. The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: People stormed and torched the town hall in Limoges, central France, destroying the 19th-century building. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People stormed and torched the town hall in Limoges, central France, destroying the 19th-century building. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images France French government in crisis talks after ‘colossal failure of the state’ Ministers, officials and police under pressure over response to days of violent unrest in cities across France Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.10 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The French government was in crisis talks on Sunday after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and more than 2000 people arrested in cities across the country . Politicians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed. The president, Emmanuel Macron , who is standing down next spring, was preparing to address the nation on Sunday night. He wrote on social media there was “no place for violence” in France. View image in fullscreen A car burns in a Paris street near graffiti reading ‘introduction to civil war’. Photograph: Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools . Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools , were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services. But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, the barricading of streets and clashing with police in cities including Paris , Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille. View image in fullscreen A protester throws a smoke flare towards gendarmes in Bordeaux, south-western France. Photograph: Christophe Archambault/AFP/Getty Images Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts. In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje. View image in fullscreen Burnt-out cars, smashed windows and the remains of barricades littered the streets of Paris on Sunday. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters In Limoges in central France , where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor, Guillaume Guérin, said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis. “Around 3:30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters because they had run out of munition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”. View image in fullscreen The mayor of Marseille, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, said questions must be asked about policing tactics. Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty Images In Marseille, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, the Socialist mayor, Benoît Payan, told BFMTV: “I have no words … I never thought I’d ever live through something like this. Hordes of rioters and looters attacked our common [state] buildings … with no real demands, but with the sole aim to wreck the demands of those who had demonstrated legitimately.” Payan said questions must be asked about policing tactics, as other town hall buildings, for example in Lille, were also targeted. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Protesters arrive to force entry into the town hall in Lille, northern France. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images Grégory Doucet, the Green mayor of Lyon, said he had never seen such violence in his city, including the torching of the historic tourist office. He told Le Monde: “I’m stunned by the violence against public and state property. I saw and heard fear and anger. Shop-owners felt abandoned.” Doucet said the government must find a “sense of nuance” in properly examining what happened and “avoiding stereotypes”. He said the government needed to give a political response to long-running societal demands from peaceful demonstrators on one hand, and also examine roots of violence. Traders’ unions said over 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked with a cost running into tens of millions of euros. “This had nothing to do with the peaceful protesters,” said one shoe-shop owner in Paris. “These were organised groups who were breaking things and looting. We’d never seen anything like it.” View image in fullscreen A protester wrapped in a French national flag stands in front of Lyon’s burning tourism office. Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty Images Opposition politicians questioned the government’s policing tactics, saying there had been a lack of state intelligence. The interior ministry said there had been more than 2,000 arrests and about 600 police, firefighters and paramedics had been hurt. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne. Macron’s centrist government and the far-right frontrunner for the presidential election, Marine Le Pen, both blamed what they called “ultra-left” groups for the violence. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would not be “intimidated” by ⁠violence, and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals. The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the peaceful street demonstration in Paris on Saturday, accused the government of organisational failings that had “opened the door to chaos”. Lecornu replied on social media: “Laying the responsibility for violence on heads of police is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibilities.” Explore more on these topics France Paris Protest Emmanuel Macron Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Why are people protesting across Europe? ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify Buildings set ablaze and more than 1,800 arrested as police clash with protesters across France ‘If we burn, you burn’: hundreds arrested at protests across France – in pictures French police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests At least 160,000 people take to streets in third week of French school protests ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state France’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned Full Story France’s teens versus the riot police – Full Story podcast Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
